subject: Environment
sub_topic: Biological Diversity Act 2002 — structure and objectives

concepts.name: Legislative Basis and International Linkage of BD Act 2002
key_dimensions: Enacted to give effect to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) 1992 — distinguishing ratification year (1994) from enactment year (2002)
Three objectives of CBD mirrored in BD Act: conservation, sustainable use, and equitable sharing of benefits
Parliamentary basis: Entry 17-A (Forests) and Entry 14 (Agriculture) of Concurrent List vs. Centre's exclusive role under Entry 63 (Union List) for regulation of wildlife
Nagoya Protocol 2010 and its relationship to the Access and Benefit Sharing provisions already present in BD Act 2002

concepts.name: Three-Tier Institutional Structure: NBA, SBBs, and BMCs
key_dimensions: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) at Centre, State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) at state level, Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) at local body level — hierarchical distinctions
UPSC trap: SBBs are constituted by STATE governments but NBA is constituted by CENTRAL government; both are statutory bodies
Overlap and conflict: which tier has jurisdiction over which category of biological resources — nationals vs. foreigners vs. NRIs
BMCs are mandatory for every local body (Panchayat/Municipality) — their role in preparation of People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs)

concepts.name: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA): Composition, Powers, and Functions
key_dimensions: Composition: Chairperson + members representing different ministries (not an elected body) — quasi-judicial and regulatory character
Headquartered in Chennai — frequently tested factual detail
Powers: grant approvals, impose conditions, receive benefit-sharing fees, take legal action for IP violations
NBA's role in granting Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) — no patent can be granted on Indian biological resources without NBA approval under Section 6

concepts.name: State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs): Jurisdiction and Conflict with NBA
key_dimensions: SBBs regulate access by Indian citizens and corporate bodies NOT covered by NBA — key jurisdictional dividing line
SBBs can only advise state governments on matters relating to biodiversity conservation; their approval powers are narrower than NBA
UPSC trap: SBBs cannot override NBA approvals; Central government can give directions to SBBs
SBBs receive a share from benefit-sharing collected by BMCs — financial flow mechanism

concepts.name: Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs): Role, Powers, and PBR Mandate
key_dimensions: Every local body MUST constitute a BMC — mandatory, not discretionary provision
Primary function: conservation, sustainable use, documentation via People's Biodiversity Register (PBR)
BMCs can levy charges on commercial users of local biological resources — but collection mechanism is often confused with NBA's benefit-sharing
BMC members are NOT elected — appointed by the local body; chairperson must be an elected member of local body (UPSC trap on this distinction)

concepts.name: People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs): Legal Status and Significance
key_dimensions: PBRs are prepared by BMCs under the BD Act — document local biological resources, their uses, and traditional knowledge
Legal status: PBRs are not themselves legal documents granting IP rights but serve as EVIDENCE of prior art against biopiracy claims
Relationship to Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) — TKDL is a separate initiative under CSIR/AYUSH, not under BD Act; frequent confusion point
PBRs as a tool for equitable benefit sharing — how their documentation feeds into NBA's benefit-sharing determinations

concepts.name: Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) Mechanism under BD Act
key_dimensions: Three-level ABS: NBA collects from foreign entities, SBBs regulate Indian companies, BMCs collect from local commercial users
Benefit sharing goes into National Biodiversity Fund / State Biodiversity Fund — purpose restricted to conservation and local community welfare
UPSC trap: ABS applies to biological resources AND associated traditional knowledge — not just physical resources
Nagoya Protocol compliance: India's BD Act predates Nagoya (2010) but is considered largely compliant; amendments have been debated

concepts.name: Sections 3, 4, and 7: The Three Prohibitions and Their Differential Applicability
key_dimensions: Section 3: Foreigners/foreign companies/NRIs require NBA PRIOR APPROVAL to obtain biological resources or knowledge — NRI inclusion is a frequent trap
Section 4: Any person (including Indian citizens) requires NBA approval before applying for ANY intellectual property right using Indian biological resources outside India
Section 7: Indian citizens and corporate bodies must GIVE PRIOR INTIMATION (not approval) to SBB for commercial utilization — weaker obligation than Section 3
Exemptions under Section 7: cultivated varieties, normally traded commodities — these are explicitly excluded from prior intimation requirement

concepts.name: Exemptions from the BD Act: Cultivated Varieties, Codified Traditional Knowledge, and Collaborative Research
key_dimensions: Section 40 exemptions: Central Government can declare certain biological resources as 'normally traded commodities' exempt from provisions
Cultivated varieties and species used by local communities for subsistence/traditional practices are exempt — but commercial scale changes the equation
Exemption for Indian researchers in collaborative research with prior approval from NBA — not a blanket exemption
UPSC trap: Vaids and traditional healers using resources for their practice are exempt; but if they commercialize, they are NOT exempt

concepts.name: Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Interface with BD Act: Section 6
key_dimensions: Section 6 mandates NBA approval before applying for IPR in India OR abroad — extraterritorial reach of the provision
Patent Controller has duty to notify NBA when a patent application involves biological resources — inter-agency coordination mechanism
BD Act vs. Patents Act 1970: biological processes are not patentable under Patents Act; BD Act adds an additional layer of regulation even for patentable inventions
Biopiracy cases (e.g., turmeric, neem, basmati) — BD Act's Section 6 as a remedial mechanism; NBA can oppose patents granted abroad

concepts.name: National Biodiversity Fund and State Biodiversity Funds: Structure and Usage
key_dimensions: National Biodiversity Fund is under NBA; State Biodiversity Funds are under respective SBBs — parallel structure
Fund sources: Central Government grants, fees from approvals, penalties, donations — not just benefit-sharing collections
Usage restrictions: conservation of biological resources, socioeconomic development of areas from which resources are drawn, benefit claimants
UPSC trap: These funds are NOT consolidated into the Consolidated Fund of India — they are separate statutory funds

concepts.name: Biodiversity Heritage Sites (BHS): Designation, Authority, and Legal Implications
key_dimensions: Section 37: State governments (in consultation with local bodies) can notify areas as Biodiversity Heritage Sites — NOT the Central Government or NBA
BHS are areas of 'significance from the point of view of biological diversity' — can include urban areas, sacred groves, agro-biodiversity hotspots
No automatic restriction on human activity unlike Protected Areas under Wildlife Protection Act — management plan prepared by state
Compensation: if BHS declaration results in loss of livelihood, state government MUST provide compensation — rarely tested but important

concepts.name: Offences, Penalties, and Enforcement Mechanism under BD Act
key_dimensions: Violations of Sections 3, 4, 7: imprisonment up to 5 years OR fine up to 10 lakh rupees OR both — quantum frequently tested
Offences under BD Act are COGNIZABLE — police can arrest without warrant; this is a significant enforcement provision
NBA has power to compound offences (Section 55) — quasi-judicial settlement power
BD Act vs. Wildlife Protection Act 1972 enforcement: WPA has dedicated enforcement officers; BD Act relies more on revenue/forest officials and NBA

concepts.name: Relationship between BD Act 2002 and Wildlife Protection Act 1972
key_dimensions: BD Act covers ALL biological resources including microorganisms, while WPA focuses on listed wild animals and plants — complementary but different scope
Protected Areas under WPA (National Parks, Sanctuaries) have STRICTER access restrictions than Biodiversity Heritage Sites under BD Act
Access to genetic resources within a Protected Area requires BOTH NBA/SBB approval AND Forest/WPA clearance — dual compliance requirement
NBA can consult with Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB) for enforcement — institutional linkage point

concepts.name: BD Act 2002 and the Forest Rights Act 2006: Convergence and Tensions
key_dimensions: Forest Rights Act recognizes community rights over biological resources of Scheduled Tribes in forests — potential overlap with BD Act's BMC jurisdiction
Gram Sabha under FRA vs. BMC under BD Act: both have roles in managing local biodiversity but different legal mandates and compositions
UPSC trap: FRA rights are INDIVIDUAL and COMMUNITY rights; BD Act creates INSTITUTIONAL mechanisms — they are not mutually exclusive but jurisdictional clarity is weak
Traditional knowledge protection: both acts address it from different angles — FRA as a rights framework, BD Act as a regulatory and benefit-sharing framework

concepts.name: Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023: Key Changes and Controversies
key_dimensions: Key change: AYUSH practitioners, local communities, and farmers using codified traditional knowledge exempted from benefit-sharing provisions — decriminalization of certain violations
Fast-track mechanism introduced for research by Indian entities — aimed at reducing compliance burden but criticized for weakening ABS
Controversy: amendments seen as diluting CBD obligations and benefiting pharmaceutical/AYUSH industry over local communities
Change in offense structure: many violations converted from criminal to civil penalties — significant shift in enforcement philosophy

concepts.name: Sovereign Rights vs. Common Heritage: Philosophical Underpinning of BD Act
key_dimensions: Pre-CBD position: biological resources were 'common heritage of mankind' (free access); CBD shifted to SOVEREIGN RIGHTS of nations over their genetic resources
BD Act operationalizes this shift — foreign entities must seek permission because India has sovereign rights over its biodiversity
Tension with TRIPS Agreement: IPR protection (TRIPS) vs. sovereign rights and ABS (CBD/BD Act) — a fundamental UPSC-level conflict
Implications for marine biodiversity: sovereign rights extend to EEZ under UNCLOS; BD Act's application to marine genetic resources is legally ambiguous

concepts.name: Traditional Knowledge and Community Rights under BD Act: Protection Mechanisms
key_dimensions: BD Act protects traditional knowledge ASSOCIATED with biological resources — not standalone cultural knowledge
Benefit sharing must flow to knowledge holders (often communities, not just individuals) — implementation challenges
UPSC trap: BD Act does NOT create a sui generis system for TK protection like proposed Geographical Indications; it only ties TK protection to biological resource access
NBA's role in opposing biopiracy patents abroad using PBRs and TKDL as prior art evidence — proactive IP defense mechanism

concepts.name: India's Biodiversity Targets and BD Act's Role: CBD COP Commitments and Kunming-Montreal Framework
key_dimensions: Aichi Biodiversity Targets (2010–2020) under CBD Strategic Plan — India's partial compliance and BD Act's role in achieving them
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022): 30x30 target — protect 30% land and sea by 2030; BD Act's Protected Area and BHS provisions as instruments
National Biodiversity Action Plan (NBAP) — prepared by MoEFCC, not by NBA; institutional distinction important
UPSC trap: India is a MEGADIVERSE country (one of 17) AND a biodiversity hotspot country (2 of 36 hotspots: Western Ghats+Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma) — these are different classification systems

concepts.name: Regulation of Research and Bio-survey under BD Act: Section 4 and Collaborative Research Provisions
key_dimensions: Any transfer of results of biological research involving Indian resources to foreign entities requires NBA approval — 'results of research' is broader than physical transfer
Collaborative research between Indian and foreign institutions requires approval but is encouraged through simplified procedures
UPSC trap: Even Indian researchers at foreign universities who conduct research on Indian biological resources are covered — nationality of researcher matters, not just institution
Distinction between bio-survey (covered) and ecological survey for non-commercial purposes (may be exempt) — line is frequently blurred in practice
